narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is substantially lower than the average ranking of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaling that your performance placed you behind most of your peers. Your first-year ranking had a similar but smaller negative effect; again, a bottom-decile position compared with an average of sixth decile among accepted applicants.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 39, it sits above the 37.2 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive contribution was not large enough to overcome the two academic-ranking signals.

Taken together, the model concluded that your overall academic trajectory made success on the bar exam slightly more likely to fail than to pass. 

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake courses or seek targeted tutoring to raise your class standing if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to push that score even higher, and then reapply. Many students improve these exact factors and gain admission on a second attempt.
